extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, educators, and researchers interested in misinformation and news literacy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for identifying, classifying, and countering 'fake news' and misinformation online, aimed at informing consumers, platforms, and researchers about detection, mitigation, and educational responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'fake news' (narrow)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrowly defined, 'fake news' means a made-up story with an intention to deceive, often geared toward getting clicks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use intent to deceive and fabrication as core markers when classifying a story as 'fake news' rather than broader categories like bias, error, or opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific-method approach to fake-news analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the scientific method to fake news analysis: Observe, Question, Hypothesize, Analyze data, Draw conclusion, and Act on results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Willingham recommends forming a hypothesis such as 'This is real news' and attempting to disprove it. Practical tests include: check the URL, date of the article, evaluate reader bias and writer bias, double-check the evidence, and verify the sources cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer fact-checker behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Educate online media consumers to themselves behave like fact-checkers — actively question the veracity of all sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach readers critical habits (e.g., verify sources, look for corroboration, question emotional or sensational claims). The Wineburg & McGrew study supports education as the solution after finding many students consistently misidentified fraudulent news as factual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check-list for verifying articles (URL/date/bias/evidence/sources)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete checks to evaluate a news item: check the URL, date of the article, evaluate reader bias and writer bias, double-check the evidence, and verify the sources cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These checks are presented as practical steps to test a hypothesis that a piece is real or fake; they are recommended as part of individual verification and fact-checking routines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorization of problematic sources (Zimdars handout)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify sources using categories like 'False, Misleading, Clickbait-y, and/or Satirical "News" Sources' rather than labeling sites simply as 'fake'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Zimdars' handout (originally for students) grouped sites into categories to guide avoidance and teaching; the list was widely circulated beyond its intended classroom use and later revised to expand and reorganize categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform mitigation: deny ad revenue to fraudulent sites
rubrics_metrics.description: Removing the ability of fraudulent sites to earn advertising revenue is a platform action aimed at reducing the motivation for producing fake news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commentators differ on sufficiency: some (e.g., Filippo Menczer) called it a good step to reduce motivation; others (e.g., Jamie Condliffe) argued banning ad revenue alone was not aggressive enough to prevent fake news from appearing in feeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform mitigation: use independent fact-checkers
rubrics_metrics.description: Platforms turning to third‑party fact-checking organizations to label or review disputed content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facebook and others began partnering with fact-checkers; this is presented as a remediation strategy but subject to debate about effectiveness and scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analytic/tracking tools to measure spread and debunking (Hoaxy example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ tools that visualize the pervasiveness of unconfirmed assertions and the related debunking activity online (example: Hoaxy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such tools help researchers and platform managers see how claims propagate and where debunking occurs, informing responses and measurement of impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus mitigation on concentrated sources and users
rubrics_metrics.description: Research shows engagement with fake-news sources is highly concentrated among a small number of websites and a tiny fraction of users; mitigation can target those concentrated nodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies cited indicate that a small share of sites and users account for a disproportionate amount of fake-news exposure and sharing, suggesting targeted interventions (e.g., shutting down networks, addressing super-spreaders) may be efficient.
